findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the disposer
findings.body: After callers invoke the returned disposer, the `"message"` handler remains registered. Later messages can still invoke stale callbacks, while repeated attach/dispose cycles retain closures and produce duplicate handling.

findings.title: [P1] Clear the polling interval during disposal
findings.body: The returned disposer no longer cancels the interval, so `refresh` continues running after teardown. This leaks timers and callback state, causes repeated post-disposal work, and can keep a Node.js process alive.

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the disposer
findings.body:
For any EventEmitter-compatible socket, calling the returned disposer no longer unsubscribes `handler`. Subsequent messages still invoke stale callbacks, and repeated attach/dispose cycles accumulate duplicate listeners.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Clear the polling interval when disposed
findings.body:
Calling the returned disposer leaves the interval active, so `refresh` continues every second after cancellation. This can cause repeated post-teardown side effects and, in Node.js, keep the process alive indefinitely.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the cleanup function no longer removes the `"message"` handler. Any later messages still invoke supposedly disposed handlers, and repeated attach/cleanup cycles accumulate duplicate listeners.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Clear the polling interval from the returned disposer
findings.body:
After callers stop polling via the returned cleanup function, `refresh` continues running every second indefinitely. This leaks the timer and closure, causes post-disposal work, and can keep Node.js processes alive.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore message-handler removal during teardown
findings.body:
A remote peer can continue triggering the handler after the caller invokes cleanup. In applications that attach per-session handlers, reconnect/logout cycles retain stale privileged closures and accumulate listeners, allowing post-session message processing and traffic-amplified CPU/memory exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Cancel the polling interval during teardown
findings.body:
Every call leaves an interval and its callback alive permanently. Where polling lifecycles can be repeatedly created—such as per client, request, or reconnect—an attacker can cause unbounded callbacks, CPU/network activity, memory retention, and prevent worker processes from exiting.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the disposer now leaves the handler registered. Repeated attach/dispose cycles on a long-lived socket retain handler closures and accumulate duplicate message processing and memory indefinitely.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Clear the polling interval during disposal
findings.body:
After `startPolling()` and its returned disposer are called, the interval still runs every second and retains `refresh`. Repeated lifecycle cycles leak timers and work; in Node.js, even one referenced interval can prevent process shutdown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
